**Case Vignette: Mrs. A.**

Mrs. A. is a 79-year-old South Asian woman, a retired airline pilot, who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of her internist. She is a slender, impeccably dressed woman who sits with a rigid posture, her hands clasped tightly in her lap. She speaks in a measured, deliberate tone, as if she is still navigating a final approach through turbulence.

Her story begins in a small town in Gujarat, India, in the late 1940s. She is the youngest of three children. Her father, a respected civil engineer, was a man of two faces. In public, he was charming and generous. At home, a door would close, and a different man would emerge. Mrs. A. remembers the specific sound of that door—a heavy, wooden latch clicking shut. It was the sound that preceded the storm.

She was seven years old. She remembers the dust motes dancing in the late afternoon light that streamed through a window. She was sitting on the cool, tiled floor, playing with a handful of colored stones. Her mother, a quiet woman with a perpetually tired look, was folding laundry. Her father came home early. Something had gone wrong at work. He was silent, a dangerous silence. Then, without a word, he crossed the room and struck her mother across the face. The sound was a sharp, wet crack. Her mother didn't cry out. She simply fell sideways onto the pile of white sheets, a small trickle of blood appearing at the corner of her mouth. Mrs. A. froze. She did not scream. She did not run. She learned to become invisible.

This was not a single event. It was the rhythm of her childhood. The pattern was always the same: a trigger (a lost contract, a burnt meal), a period of coiled tension, the explosion, and then the long, silent aftermath where her mother would move through the house like a ghost. Mrs. A. learned to read the air for pressure changes. She became a master of hypervigilance. She would watch her father’s hands, the set of his jaw, the way he held his tea cup. She would listen for the change in his breathing. She learned that safety was a fragile, temporary state.

She escaped into the sky. She was the first woman in her region to earn a commercial pilot’s license. In the cockpit, she found a world of order, checklists, and predictable physics. There was no ambiguity. Ailerons, rudders, altimeters—they all followed rules. It was the opposite of home. She flew for 45 years. She was known for her calm under pressure, for her ability to land a 747 in a crosswind without a tremor. Her colleagues called her “the Ice Queen” with affection. She never told them that the calm was a learned response, a dissociation that had become a professional asset. When a warning light flashed on the instrument panel, she did not feel fear. She felt a strange, familiar clarity. She simply detached from her body and became a machine for problem-solving.

Now, at 79, she has been retired for 14 years. The sky is gone. She lives with her husband, a gentle, retired professor, in a quiet suburban home. He is a good man, a kind man. He has never raised his voice to her. And yet, she cannot relax. Every small, unexpected noise—a dropped spoon, a car backfiring, a door that slams a little too hard—sends a current through her. Her heart races. Her throat closes. She feels the cold tile floor of her childhood under her hands. She avoids the kitchen when her husband is chopping vegetables. The rhythmic thud of the knife is too much.

She has terrible nightmares, but she does not call them that. She tells me she has “troubled sleep.” In the dreams, she is always seven years old, but she is also the pilot. She is trying to land a plane in a storm, but the instruments are all wrong. The altimeter is spinning backward. The runway is her childhood home. She wakes up gasping, her body rigid, her husband’s hand on her shoulder, asking if she is okay. She says she is fine. She says this so often it has become her name.

She cannot watch movies with conflict. She leaves the room during the news. She has stopped visiting her children, because their homes feel too full of unpredictable variables—a child’s sudden shriek, a slammed door. She has shrunk her world to a very small cockpit. She tells me, with a dry, almost clinical detachment, “I am not in danger. I know this. My body does not know this.” Her hands are still clasped tightly in her lap.
